intro: Foundations of International Law. Unit six: states, diplomatic protection, succession, and immunity.

slides.3: The three-elements doctrine. What makes a state is answered by the three-elements doctrine, and by Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933: a permanent population, a defined territory, and a government. The Convention adds a fourth qualification, the capacity to enter into relations with other states — held here in square brackets, because it is contested: it arguably describes a consequence of statehood rather than a condition of it.
slides.4: The population element. The permanent population is defined by the legal bond of nationality, and that bond is described through its content: nationals have the right of residence and return, and the right to take part in political decision-making; and they owe tax duties and military service. Rights and duties both — which is exactly the structure the Nottebohm case will use to test whether a nationality is real.
slides.6: Nationality of companies. For legal persons there is no birth and no descent, so international practice uses four possible connecting factors: the law under which the entity was founded, its registration, its seat, and control over it. Which factor applies decides who may protect the company — and the Barcelona Traction case, coming shortly, shows which two the International Court of Justice chose.
slides.11: Exhaustion of local remedies: the rule. The Interhandel case states it as well-established customary law: local remedies must be exhausted before international proceedings may be instituted, because the state where the violation occurred should have the opportunity to redress it by its own means, within its own legal system. That rationale is what makes the exceptions intelligible — if the opportunity is illusory, the rule has no work to do.
slides.14: The Calvo doctrine — a Latin American answer to diplomatic protection: foreign investors should be treated equally with nationals, and should have recourse only to local courts. Contracts accordingly contained Calvo clauses, in which the investor waived the right to seek diplomatic protection. And here is the doctrinal problem with that: since the right of protection belongs to the state and not to the investor, an investor cannot validly waive what is not theirs to give up.
slides.15: The territory element. State territory covers the land surface, the territorial sea and internal waters, and the airspace above them. Two further items go with it: the problem of demarcation, and the uti possidetis principle, under which a new state inherits the administrative boundaries that existed before independence. That is the rule which kept colonial borders in place across Africa and Latin America, and which then applied again to the former Yugoslavia.
slides.16: State authority and its limits. The third element is the power to regulate, and international law limits it by requiring sufficient proximity between the regulating state and the matter regulated. Where several states each have a claim to regulate, the conflict rules step in: private international law, international criminal law, and international administrative law. The criminal-law list comes next, and that is the one exams use.
slides.18: Recognition of states. The position taken here settles the old debate: recognition is only declaratory, not constitutive. An entity is a state because it meets the three elements, not because others say so. Recognition may be express, by formal letter or diplomatic note, or implied, by establishing diplomatic relations or concluding a bilateral treaty. And two things are expressly not implied recognition: admitting the entity to an international organization, since admission can be decided by majority against the will of some members; and ratifying a multilateral treaty to which it is also party.
slides.21: The law of succession: two Vienna Conventions and customary law. The 1978 Convention on Succession of States in respect of Treaties; the 1983 Convention on Succession in respect of State Property, Archives and Debts; and custom. Both conventions have few parties, so in practice the customary position does most of the work — which is why the competing basic positions, coming next, matter.
slides.29: Distomo, in Greece: immunity denied. The Greek Supreme Court held that the tort exception applied even to claims arising out of military operations, where the acts breached a peremptory rule of international law. The reasoning is attractive — a jus cogens violation cannot be a protected sovereign act — and it is the argument to know. It is also the argument that lost: the International Court of Justice later took the same view as Germany, in Jurisdictional Immunities of the State, 2012.
slides.38: Transnational corporations. The 1988 United Nations Code of Conduct defines one as an enterprise comprising entities in two or more countries, whatever their legal form and field of activity, operating under a system of decision-making that permits coherent policies and a common strategy through one or more decision-making centres, the entities being so linked by ownership or otherwise that one or more may exercise significant influence over the others and share knowledge, resources and responsibilities. The definition looks to control, not to corporate form — which is why the nationality of companies is such a difficult question.
